specStatements.text: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions. The amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings the product molecules must have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
An exothermic reaction is one that transfers energy to the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
Exothermic reactions include combustion, many oxidation reactions and neutralisation.
Everyday uses of exothermic reactions include self-heating cans and hand warmers.
An endothermic reaction is one that takes in energy from the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Endothermic reactions include thermal decompositions and the reaction of citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate. Some sports injury packs are based on endothermic reactions.
Students should be able to:
distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions on the basis of the temperature change of the surroundings
evaluate uses and applications of exothermic and endothermic reactions given appropriate information.
Limited to measurement of temperature change. Calculation of energy changes or ΔH is not required.
Required practical 4: investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions such as, eg acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations, displacement of metals.

Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy.
Reaction profiles can be used to show the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change of a reaction.
Students should be able to:

draw simple reaction profiles (energy level diagrams) for exothermic and endothermic reactions showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change, with a curved line to show the energy as the reaction proceeds
use reaction profiles to identify reactions as exothermic or endothermic
explain that the activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
During a chemical reaction:
energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants
energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
The energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed can be calculated from bond energies.

The difference between the sum of the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants and the sum of the energy released when bonds in the products are formed is the overall energy change of the reaction.
In an exothermic reaction, the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.
In an endothermic reaction, the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds.

scopeNotes.statement: Limited to measurement of temperature change.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Everything under 4.5.1.1, including Required practical 4, is judged by the temperature of the surroundings before and after the reaction - a rise or a fall read from a thermometer. No item asks students to turn a temperature change into a quantity of energy, and none uses mass, specific heat capacity or the expression for energy transferred. Where numbers in kilojoules appear on a reaction profile they are read directly off the labelled diagram, which 4.5.1.2 requires; they are never derived from a temperature measurement.

scopeNotes.statement: Calculation of energy changes or ΔH is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The symbol ΔH is not used anywhere in this content, and no item under 4.5.1.1 asks for an energy change to be calculated. Energy-change values in kJ/mol appear only under 4.5.1.3, where the specification does require them to be worked out from bond energies, and that material is marked Higher tier throughout. There the quantity is always called the overall energy change, in the specification's own words.

concepts.term: Conservation of energy in chemical reactions
concepts.definition: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions. The amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place; energy is only transferred between the reacting chemicals and their surroundings.

concepts.term: Energy of the products compared with the reactants
concepts.definition: If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, the product molecules must have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred. Nothing is destroyed: the missing energy is now in the surroundings.

Everything other than the reacting chemicals themselves - the solvent, the container and the air around it. When a reaction is carried out in solution, a thermometer in the mixture is reading the temperature of the surroundings.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Burning a substance in oxygen. Combustion reactions are exothermic: burning methane in a Bunsen burner transfers energy to the surroundings.
Reactions in which a substance gains oxygen. Many oxidation reactions are exothermic - the oxidation of iron inside a hand warmer is one - although the specification says many, not all.
The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to make a salt and water. Neutralisation is exothermic, so mixing an acid and an alkali raises the temperature of the solution.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction. Reactants held separately in the base of the can are mixed by the user, and the energy transferred to the surroundings warms the drink.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction. A reaction inside the pack, such as the oxidation of iron once air is let in, transfers energy to the surroundings and so to the user's hands.

Breaking a compound down into simpler substances by heating it, for example calcium carbonate to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Thermal decompositions are endothermic: energy has to be taken in continuously for them to keep going.
A named endothermic reaction. When the two are mixed the mixture fizzes and its temperature falls, because energy is taken in from the surroundings.
Some sports injury packs are based on endothermic reactions. Squeezing the pack mixes the contents, energy is taken in from the surroundings, and the pack becomes cold enough to treat an injury.

Measure the temperature of the surroundings before and after the reaction. A temperature rise shows the reaction is exothermic; a temperature fall shows it is endothermic. It is the direction of the change that decides, not its size.

Weighing an exothermic or endothermic product against the information you are given - the temperature it reaches, how long the effect lasts, whether it can be reused, cost and safety - and then reaching a judgement that the data supports.

An investigation of the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, such as acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations or displacement of metals. The reaction is carried out in an insulated container and the temperature is recorded before and after.

The independent variable is what you deliberately change, for example the volume of alkali added. The dependent variable is the temperature you measure. Control variables, such as the volume and concentration of the acid, are kept the same so the comparison is fair.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. Particles that collide with too little energy simply bounce apart unchanged.

The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is the energy needed for a reaction to occur, and it must be supplied before any reaction happens, whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall.

An energy level diagram used to show the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change of a reaction, with a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products. On a reaction profile it is the vertical gap between the reactant level and the product level, not the height of the peak.

Reactants on the left, products on the right, joined by a curved line that rises to a peak and then falls. The activation energy is measured from the reactant level up to the peak; the overall energy change is measured between the reactant level and the product level. Products sit below the reactants for an exothermic reaction and above them for an endothermic one.

concepts.term: Reading exothermic or endothermic from a profile
concepts.definition: If the products are lower than the reactants, energy has been transferred to the surroundings and the reaction is exothermic. If the products are higher than the reactants, energy has been taken in and the reaction is endothermic.
Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so breaking bonds is an endothermic process.
Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed, so making bonds is an exothermic process.

The energy associated with a particular bond, from which the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed can be calculated. Every bond present must be counted, including the extra molecules shown by the numbers in front of the formulae in the balanced equation.

concepts.term: Overall energy change from bond energies
concepts.definition: The difference between the sum of the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants and the sum of the energy released when bonds in the products are formed. A negative value means the reaction is exothermic and a positive value means it is endothermic.

concepts.term: Exothermic reactions in terms of bonds
concepts.definition: In an exothermic reaction, the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds, so there is energy left over to transfer to the surroundings.

concepts.term: Endothermic reactions in terms of bonds
concepts.definition: In an endothermic reaction, the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds, so the shortfall has to be taken in from the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: A beaker of reacting solution gets hot. Is energy going into the reaction or out of it?
misconceptions.correct: Out of it. The reaction is exothermic: energy is transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings, which is why the surroundings get hotter.
misconceptions.misconception: If something gets hot it must be taking energy in, so a reaction that heats a beaker is endothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday life things get hot because you heat them - a kettle, an oven, a radiator. Students carry that pattern over and assume the hot object is the one receiving energy, which reverses the meaning of the two words.
misconceptions.correction: Always ask which way the arrow points relative to the surroundings. Exothermic sends energy out to the surroundings, and it is the surroundings you are measuring with the thermometer, so a rise means energy came out.

misconceptions.question: If an exothermic reaction gives energy away, does the beaker end up colder?
misconceptions.correct: No. The energy given away goes into the surroundings, and the surroundings include the solution the thermometer is in, so the reading rises.
misconceptions.misconception: Giving out energy means losing it, so everything involved ends up cooler than before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think about the reacting chemicals rather than the surroundings, and 'losing energy' sounds like cooling. The specification defines both terms by what happens to the surroundings, not to the chemicals.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two systems. The chemicals do end up with less energy - the products have less energy than the reactants - but the surroundings have gained exactly that amount, so the surroundings warm up.

misconceptions.question: A hand warmer gets hot for six hours and then goes cold. Has that energy been used up?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy is conserved: the amount of energy in the universe at the end of the reaction is the same as before. The energy has spread into the air and the user's hands.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactions use energy up, so after an exothermic reaction there is less energy in the world than there was.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks about fuel being used up and batteries going flat, which makes energy sound like a stock that can be exhausted rather than something that is transferred.
misconceptions.correction: Track where the energy went instead of asking how much is left. It moved from the chemical store in the reactants to the surroundings; the total is unchanged, which is exactly what conservation of energy means.

misconceptions.question: An exothermic reaction releases energy. Do the products have more energy than the reactants?
misconceptions.correct: No, less. If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, the product molecules must have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction produced energy, so the products must be the energy-rich things at the end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'releases energy' as 'gains energy' and picture the products as the outcome of a build-up. Diagrams that are drawn without axis labels make it easy to see the products as the endpoint of a rise.
misconceptions.correction: Use the conservation argument. The energy transferred out has to come from somewhere, and the only place it can come from is the chemicals, so the products must be lower in energy by exactly that amount.

misconceptions.question: Energy is conserved in a reaction. Does that mean reactants and products have the same energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Conservation applies to the universe as a whole, not to the chemicals alone. The products can have less energy than the reactants provided the surroundings have gained the difference.
misconceptions.misconception: If energy is conserved, then the energy before and after must be equal on both sides of the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is taught first, and there the two sides really do balance. Students apply the same bookkeeping to energy and forget that the surroundings are part of the account.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the boundary wider. Write chemicals plus surroundings on each side: it is that total which is unchanged, which allows the chemicals alone to lose or gain energy.

misconceptions.question: Does energy only stay conserved if the reaction is in a sealed container?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy is conserved in every chemical reaction. A sealed container only makes it easier to keep track of the energy, it does not change whether energy is conserved.
misconceptions.misconception: In an open beaker energy escapes and is lost, so conservation only really applies in a closed system.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Practical work stresses insulation and lids to stop energy 'escaping', and conservation of mass genuinely does need a closed system to demonstrate. The two ideas get merged.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish losing track of energy from losing energy. Energy that leaves an open beaker is in the room; it still exists, so the total in the universe is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: You have to light a Bunsen burner with a match. Does that make combustion endothermic?
misconceptions.correct: No. Combustion is exothermic. The match only supplies the activation energy needed to start it; once burning, the reaction transfers far more energy to the surroundings than the match supplied.
misconceptions.misconception: You have to put energy in to make it burn, so burning takes energy in overall.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first energy transfer a student notices is the one they carry out themselves. The activation energy is visible and deliberate, while the much larger release afterwards is taken for granted.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what happens after the match is removed. An endothermic reaction stops when you stop heating it; a burning Bunsen keeps going and heats the room, which is only possible if energy is coming out.

misconceptions.question: Acid and alkali cancel each other out in neutralisation. Is there no energy change?
misconceptions.correct: There is. Neutralisation is exothermic: mixing an acid and an alkali raises the temperature of the solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutralisation just cancels the acid and the alkali, so nothing is gained or lost and the temperature stays the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'neutral' suggests nothing happening, and pH work presents neutralisation as an arithmetic cancelling of opposites rather than as a chemical reaction that makes new bonds.
misconceptions.correction: Point out that new substances - a salt and water - are formed, and that forming them releases energy. This is why a titration flask feels warm and why the specification lists neutralisation as exothermic.

misconceptions.question: Calcium carbonate is heated strongly in a furnace. Is that an exothermic reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is endothermic. Thermal decompositions take in energy from the surroundings, which is why the heating has to continue for the reaction to continue.
misconceptions.misconception: The furnace is red hot, so the reaction inside it must be giving out energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge from the temperature of the apparatus rather than the direction of transfer, and heat is so obviously present that it is assumed to be coming from the reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Ask who is supplying the energy. Turn the furnace off and the decomposition stops, showing the reaction is a consumer of energy, not a source of it.

misconceptions.question: Citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate fizz violently. Does that show energy is being given out?
misconceptions.correct: No. This reaction is endothermic - the temperature of the mixture falls, even though it fizzes vigorously.
misconceptions.misconception: A vigorous, fizzing reaction must be exothermic, because it looks energetic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bubbling looks dramatic, and students associate visible activity with energy being released. Rate and energy change are two different things, but they are easily conflated.
misconceptions.correction: Put a thermometer in it. The fizzing tells you carbon dioxide is being made quickly; only the temperature of the surroundings tells you which way energy is being transferred.

misconceptions.question: The mixture cools as gas bubbles out. Has the gas carried the heat away?
misconceptions.correct: No. The cooling happens because the reaction itself takes in energy from the surroundings. The escaping gas is a product of the reaction, not a route for the energy to leave.
misconceptions.misconception: Bubbles rising out of the beaker carry the warmth away with them, which is why the reading drops.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is a tempting mechanical explanation that fits everyday experience of steam leaving a pan, and it lets students avoid accepting that a reaction can absorb energy.
misconceptions.correction: Compare with a fizzing exothermic reaction, such as a carbonate with acid in a warm mixture, where gas also escapes and the temperature still rises. The gas is not what decides the direction.

misconceptions.question: Does a hand warmer work by trapping the heat from your hands?
misconceptions.correct: No. A chemical reaction inside the pack, such as the oxidation of iron, is exothermic and transfers energy to the surroundings, so the pack is a source of energy rather than an insulator.
misconceptions.misconception: The pack is just good insulation - it holds in your body heat, which is why your hands feel warm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gloves and pockets do work exactly this way, so insulation is the familiar explanation. Nothing visible happens inside the pack to suggest a reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Leave the pack on a bench with nobody touching it. It still becomes hot, and it eventually stops working even though it is still just as well insulated, because the reactants have been used up.

misconceptions.question: Hand warmer A reaches 58 °C for one hour, B reaches 42 °C for seven hours. Is A the better product?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Evaluating an application means weighing all the information given - the temperature reached, how long it lasts, whether it can be reused, cost and safety - not just the peak temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The one that gets hottest is the best hand warmer, because it gives out the most energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Peak temperature is the single number students are used to comparing, and evaluation questions look like a search for the biggest value rather than a judgement.
misconceptions.correction: Match the product to the stated use. For a day on a mountain, seven hours at 42 °C beats one hour at 58 °C; a temperature of 58 °C may also be a burn risk against bare skin.

misconceptions.question: A hand warmer can be reset in boiling water and used again. Does that make its reaction endothermic?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is exothermic in use - it transfers energy to the surroundings and gets hot. Being reusable says something about whether the change can be reversed, not about the direction of the energy transfer while it is working.
misconceptions.misconception: If it lasts a long time or can be recharged, the reaction must be taking energy in rather than giving it out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear 'takes energy in' when they see the pack being boiled, and attach that label to the whole product rather than to the separate resetting step.
misconceptions.correction: Classify one process at a time. While the warmer is warming your hands the surroundings get hotter, so that reaction is exothermic; putting it in boiling water afterwards is a different change.

misconceptions.question: Must a sports injury cold pack contain ice or a refrigerant?
misconceptions.correct: No. Some sports injury packs are based on endothermic reactions: mixing the contents takes energy in from the surroundings, so the pack becomes cold without ever having been cooled.
misconceptions.misconception: Something can only be cold if it was refrigerated first, so the pack must have ice or a coolant sealed inside it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every cold thing a student has met was made cold by a freezer. The idea that a chemical change can produce coldness on demand has no everyday parallel.
misconceptions.correction: Note that the pack is stored at room temperature and only becomes cold when squeezed. The coldness appears at the moment the chemicals mix, which is exactly what an endothermic reaction does.

misconceptions.question: One reaction warms a cup by 20 °C and another by 4 °C. Is the first one faster?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. The size of the temperature change tells you about the energy transferred, not about how quickly the reaction happened. Both are exothermic because both got warmer.
misconceptions.misconception: A big temperature change means a fast reaction and a small one means a slow reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In practice a fast exothermic reaction often does feel more dramatic, and students meet rate and energy change in the same practical work, so the two measures get fused.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what was measured. Rate needs a time; the thermometer reading is a total, and a slow reaction left for long enough can produce a large temperature change.

misconceptions.question: Reaction W warms the surroundings by 11 °C and reaction X cools them by 6 °C. Which is endothermic?
misconceptions.correct: X. Endothermic means the temperature of the surroundings decreases, so it is the direction of the change that decides, not how large the change is.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction with the biggest temperature change is the exothermic or endothermic one - you compare the numbers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students trained to look for the largest value in a table read off magnitudes and skip the sign. Data is often presented as 'temperature change' without a minus sign to make the direction obvious.
misconceptions.correction: Write each result as 'rose' or 'fell' before comparing anything. Rose means exothermic, fell means endothermic; only then does the size of the change tell you anything further.

misconceptions.question: Why is a polystyrene cup used in Required practical 4 rather than a glass beaker?
misconceptions.correct: Because polystyrene is a good insulator, so it reduces the energy transferred between the mixture and the surroundings and gives a more valid temperature change.
misconceptions.misconception: Polystyrene is used because it does not react with the acid, unlike glass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Choosing apparatus for chemical resistance is a familiar idea from other practicals, and glass is in fact unreactive too, so the reasoning is never tested by experience.
misconceptions.correction: Point out that glass is also unreactive but conducts energy away far faster. Adding a lid, which cannot affect reactivity at all, improves the result for the same reason - it reduces energy transfer.

misconceptions.question: Do all collisions between reacting particles cause a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Reactions occur only when particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. A collision with less than the activation energy leaves the particles unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: If the right particles bump into each other they will react - that is what a reaction is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The collision picture is introduced first and is intuitive; the energy condition is an extra clause that is easy to drop, especially as students cannot see the unsuccessful collisions.
misconceptions.correction: State both conditions together every time: they must collide, and they must collide with at least the activation energy. Most collisions in a room-temperature mixture achieve neither reaction nor change.

misconceptions.question: Is the activation energy the energy a reaction gives out?
misconceptions.correct: No. The activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react - the energy needed for a reaction to occur, supplied before anything happens.
misconceptions.misconception: Activation energy is the energy the reaction produces once it becomes active.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'activation' suggests the reaction springing into life, and students associate that moment with energy being given out rather than with a barrier that must first be climbed.
misconceptions.correction: Locate it on a reaction profile: it is the climb from the reactants up to the peak, before any product exists. What the reaction gives out is a different quantity, the overall energy change.

misconceptions.question: Is the activation energy the gap between the reactants and the products?
misconceptions.correct: No. That gap is the overall energy change. The activation energy is measured from the reactant level up to the peak of the curve.
misconceptions.misconception: Activation energy and overall energy change are two names for the same distance on the diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are vertical distances measured in kJ/mol on the same diagram, and unlabelled sketches make them easy to confuse.
misconceptions.correction: Label both on one profile. The activation energy always starts at the reactant level and ends at the peak; the overall energy change always runs from the reactant level to the product level.

misconceptions.question: Exothermic reactions give out energy. Do they still need an activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Every reaction needs particles to collide with at least the activation energy before it can occur, however much energy it gives out afterwards.
misconceptions.misconception: Only endothermic reactions need energy putting in; an exothermic reaction has energy to spare, so it starts on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The overall energy change is the headline fact students remember about an exothermic reaction, and it seems contradictory that a reaction which releases energy should also require some.
misconceptions.correction: Use petrol as the example. It is strongly exothermic yet sits safely in a tank until a spark supplies the activation energy - which is precisely why the barrier must exist.

misconceptions.question: What is plotted along the bottom of a reaction profile?
misconceptions.correct: The progress of the reaction, from reactants on the left to products on the right. Energy is plotted up the vertical axis.
misconceptions.misconception: The horizontal axis is time, so the diagram shows how the reaction speeds up and slows down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every other graph in science has time along the bottom, and the curve does look like something changing as the reaction runs.
misconceptions.correction: Read the axis label. The curve shows the energy as the reaction proceeds, not how long anything takes; nothing on a reaction profile tells you the rate.

misconceptions.question: A profile shows reactants at 250 kJ/mol and a peak at 400 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: 150 kJ/mol. The activation energy is measured from the reactant level up to the peak, so it is 400 - 250.
misconceptions.misconception: The activation energy is the height of the peak above the bottom of the axis, so it is 400 kJ/mol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read heights off a graph in the usual way, from the axis upwards, and the peak is the most obvious feature on the diagram.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the arrow before reading any number. It starts on the reactant line, not on the axis, because the particles already have the reactants' energy before they collide.

misconceptions.question: Can a reaction profile be drawn as a straight line from reactants to products?
misconceptions.correct: No. It must be drawn with a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds, rising to a peak that represents the activation energy before falling to the product level.
misconceptions.misconception: The diagram just needs the two energy levels joined up, so a sloping line between them is enough.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the diagram as a comparison of two levels and treat the joining line as decoration, especially when they have only ever been asked whether products are higher or lower.
misconceptions.correction: Remember that the peak carries information. Without the curve there is nowhere to show the activation energy, and the specification requires a curved line in every profile that is drawn.

misconceptions.question: Where are the products drawn on the profile of an exothermic reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Below the reactants. Energy has been transferred to the surroundings, so the products have less energy than the reactants.
misconceptions.misconception: Exothermic reactions give out energy, so their products are drawn higher up the energy axis.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Giving out' is heard as 'having more', and up on a diagram is read as more of everything. Without linking the diagram to conservation of energy there is nothing to correct the guess.
misconceptions.correction: Tie the picture to the definition. The energy in the surroundings went up, so the energy of the chemicals must have gone down; an exothermic profile therefore steps downwards from left to right.

misconceptions.question: Does breaking a chemical bond release energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking is endothermic. Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
misconceptions.misconception: Bonds store energy, so breaking them lets that energy out - like snapping a stretched elastic band.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday talk about explosives and food 'releasing the energy stored in their bonds' says exactly this, and it feels right that destroying something should give energy back.
misconceptions.correction: Think of the bond as an attraction that has to be pulled apart, which always costs energy. The energy released in burning comes from making the strong new bonds in carbon dioxide and water, not from breaking the old ones.

misconceptions.question: Does forming the bonds in the products use energy up?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed. It is breaking bonds that requires energy to be supplied.
misconceptions.misconception: Making something new must take energy, so building the product molecules costs energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Construction is effortful in ordinary life, so building a molecule sounds like work. The exact reversal of the two processes is a hard idea to hold on to under exam pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the pair as one sentence and never separate them: energy in to break, energy out to make. Checking a known exothermic reaction with real bond energies confirms it every time.

misconceptions.question: How is the overall energy change worked out from bond energies?
misconceptions.correct: It is the difference between the sum of the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants and the sum of the energy released when bonds in the products are formed - bonds broken minus bonds formed.
misconceptions.misconception: You take the energy released making bonds and subtract the energy needed to break them, since the release is what you are interested in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students subtract the smaller number from the larger to avoid a negative answer, and doing so happens to reverse the sign in exactly the cases where the sign matters most.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the order as reactants first, products second, and let the sign do the work: a negative answer means exothermic, a positive answer means endothermic. Then check the sign against whether the mixture would get hotter.

misconceptions.question: For H2 + Br2 → 2HBr, how many H-Br bonds are formed?
misconceptions.correct: Two. The 2 in front of HBr means two molecules are made, each containing one H-Br bond, so the energy released is 2 x the H-Br bond energy.
misconceptions.misconception: You add one bond energy for each substance in the equation, so the H-Br value is counted once.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bond energy tables list one value per bond type, which invites one entry per row. The multipliers in front of the formulae are read as labels rather than as instructions to count again.
misconceptions.correction: Write out every molecule and every bond before touching the table. Multiply each bond energy by the number of those bonds present, using the numbers in front of the formulae and the subscripts inside them.

misconceptions.question: A reaction makes more bonds than it breaks. Does that make it exothermic?
misconceptions.correct: Not by itself. What matters is the energy: in an exothermic reaction the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds. Bonds differ in strength, so counting them is not enough.
misconceptions.misconception: Count the bonds on each side - more bonds in the products means energy is given out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting is easier than adding energies, and it does often give the right answer, which makes the shortcut hard to dislodge.
misconceptions.correction: Compare a case where a few very strong bonds outweigh many weak ones. The specification asks for the sums of energies, so always add the kJ/mol values rather than counting lines.

misconceptions.question: Is energy supplied both to break bonds and to make them?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, but energy is released when bonds in the products are formed. The two processes run in opposite directions.
misconceptions.misconception: Every step of a reaction needs energy putting in, so both breaking and making bonds take energy from the surroundings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The activation energy is always supplied at the start, so students generalise that energy input is what drives the whole process, and never picture any step giving energy back.
misconceptions.correction: If both steps took energy in, no reaction could ever be exothermic. The energy transferred to the surroundings by a fire has to come from the bond making step.

misconceptions.question: A sports injury pack becomes cold. Has it released cold into the surroundings?
misconceptions.correct: No. Cold is not a substance that can be released. The endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, and the surroundings become colder because that energy has left them.
misconceptions.misconception: Cold flows out of the pack into your skin, in the same way that heat flows out of a hand warmer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heat and cold are treated as opposite substances in everyday speech - people talk about letting the cold in. Only one of them, energy, actually moves.
misconceptions.correction: Describe every case as energy moving in one direction only. The pack feels cold because energy is moving from your skin into the pack, not because anything is coming out of it.

misconceptions.question: Does the warmth of a hand warmer come from salt dissolving in the water?
misconceptions.correct: No. The exothermic change is the oxidation of the iron, which is a chemical reaction. The salt is there to speed that reaction up, not to supply the energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Dissolving always warms a solution, so the salt dissolving is what heats the pack.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Salt and water are the recognisable ingredients on the packet, and students have seen dissolving produce temperature changes, so it is the obvious candidate.
misconceptions.correction: Look at what is used up. A hand warmer stops working when the iron has turned to rust, and it only starts when air is let in - both point to oxidation of the iron as the source.

misconceptions.question: In Required practical 4 you measure the temperature after each addition of alkali. Is temperature the independent variable?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is the dependent variable. The independent variable is the volume of alkali you deliberately add; the temperature is what you measure in response.
misconceptions.misconception: The independent variable is the one you read off the equipment, because that is the one you collect data for.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The measured quantity is the focus of the practical and fills the results table, so it feels like the important, and therefore the independent, variable.
misconceptions.correction: Ask which one you chose before starting. You decided on 5 cm3 portions, so that is independent; the thermometer reading depended on your choice, so it is dependent.

misconceptions.question: If you add more alkali each time, should you add more acid too?
misconceptions.correct: No. The volume and concentration of the acid are control variables and must be kept the same, or you cannot tell what caused any change in temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: To keep it fair you should increase both, so the two solutions stay in step with each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Fair test' is sometimes remembered as treating everything equally, rather than as changing exactly one variable and holding the rest constant.
misconceptions.correction: Change one thing only. If both volumes rise together, a change in temperature could be caused by either, and the results cannot answer the question you set.

misconceptions.question: Does using an insulated cup with a lid make the reaction release more energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. The reaction releases the same energy either way. The insulation stops so much of it escaping to the room, so a larger share of it warms the mixture and the measured temperature change is closer to the true value.
misconceptions.misconception: Insulating the cup makes the reaction more exothermic, which is why the temperature rise is bigger.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The observed rise really is bigger with a lid on, and the simplest explanation of a bigger reading is a bigger reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the reaction from the measurement. Nothing about the chemicals has changed; the lid only changes how much of the transferred energy stays where the thermometer can detect it.

misconceptions.question: Must every particle have the activation energy before a reaction can happen?
misconceptions.correct: No. A reaction occurs whenever particles collide with each other with sufficient energy. Only the colliding pair needs to have at least the activation energy between them.
misconceptions.misconception: The whole mixture has to be heated up to the activation energy before anything reacts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating a mixture is described as 'giving it the activation energy', which sounds like a threshold the bulk sample must reach, as though it were a melting point.
misconceptions.correction: Treat it as a condition on each collision, not on the sample. Some particles always have more energy than others, so a few collisions succeed even in a mixture that is not being heated.

misconceptions.question: Does the vertical axis of a reaction profile show temperature?
misconceptions.correct: No, it shows energy. The profile shows the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change.
misconceptions.misconception: Since exothermic and endothermic reactions are about temperature changes, the axis going up the diagram must be temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature is the measurement used throughout 4.5.1.1 to classify reactions, so it is the quantity students expect to see when a diagram appears.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two representations apart. Temperature is what you measure in the surroundings to classify a reaction; the profile shows the energy of the chemicals themselves as the reaction proceeds.

mcqs.stem: A reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. What does this tell you about the product molecules?

options.text: They have more energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'releases energy' as 'gains energy' and picture the products as the energy-rich end of the change.

options.text: They have exactly the same energy as the reactants, as energy is conserved.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass balances both sides of an equation, and students apply the same bookkeeping to energy, forgetting the surroundings.

options.text: They have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
options.rationale: This is the specification's own statement: the energy transferred out came from the chemicals, so the products must be lower in energy by exactly that amount.

options.text: They have less energy, and that energy no longer exists anywhere.
options.rationale: Half right, but it treats the transferred energy as used up rather than moved into the surroundings.

mcqs.stem: An exothermic reaction is carried out in an open beaker. What happens to the total amount of energy in the universe?

options.text: It is the same as before; the energy has moved to the surroundings.
options.rationale: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions: the amount in the universe at the end is the same as before the reaction takes place.

options.text: It is lower than before, because the reaction has used energy up.
options.rationale: Everyday talk of fuel being used up makes energy sound like a stock that can be exhausted rather than transferred.

options.text: It depends on whether the container was sealed during the reaction.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass genuinely does need a closed system to demonstrate, so students transfer that condition to energy.

options.text: It is higher than before, because the reaction has made new energy.
options.rationale: Picked by students who take 'the reaction produces energy' literally, treating the reaction as a source rather than a route.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?

options.text: Energy is transferred to the surroundings, whose temperature rises.
options.rationale: This is the definition: an exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings increases.

options.text: Energy is taken in from the surroundings, whose temperature falls.
options.rationale: This is the definition of an endothermic reaction, selected by students who attach 'exo-' to energy going in.

options.text: Energy is transferred to the surroundings, whose temperature falls.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who reason that giving energy away must leave everything cooler, including the surroundings that received it.

options.text: Energy is taken in from the surroundings, whose temperature rises.
options.rationale: Attractive to students who reason from everyday heating - things get hot because energy is put into them.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an exothermic reaction?

options.text: Heating calcium carbonate to form calcium oxide
options.rationale: Students judge from the hot furnace and assume the reaction is a source of energy; thermal decompositions are in fact endothermic.

options.text: Adding citric acid to sodium hydrogencarbonate
options.rationale: The vigorous fizzing looks energetic, so it is read as energy being given out, although the temperature actually falls.

options.text: Magnesium burning in air to form magnesium oxide
options.rationale: This is both a combustion and an oxidation reaction, and the specification lists combustion and many oxidation reactions as exothermic.

options.text: The reaction inside a sports injury cold pack
options.rationale: Chosen by students who group all commercial packs together with hand warmers and assume every one of them warms up.

mcqs.stem: A hand warmer contains iron powder, salt and water. It becomes hot a few minutes after the outer wrapper is opened. Why?

options.text: The pack traps energy from the hands and stops it escaping again.
options.rationale: Gloves and pockets really do work this way, so insulation is the familiar explanation for anything that feels warm.

options.text: The iron is oxidised, and this exothermic reaction transfers energy out.
options.rationale: Opening the wrapper lets air in, and the oxidation of the iron is exothermic, so energy is transferred to the surroundings.

options.text: An endothermic reaction takes energy in, which makes the pack hot.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a hot object must be one that is receiving energy, which reverses the two definitions.

options.text: The salt dissolving in the water is what releases all the energy.
options.rationale: Salt and water are the recognisable ingredients, and students have seen dissolving change a temperature.

mcqs.stem: Two solutions are mixed in a test tube and the outside of the tube quickly feels cold. What is happening?

options.text: The reaction is releasing cold into the surroundings around it.
options.rationale: Everyday speech treats cold as a substance that can flow, so students picture it leaving the tube.

options.text: The reaction is taking energy in from the surroundings, which cool.
options.rationale: This is an endothermic reaction: energy is taken in from the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

options.text: The reaction is exothermic, since the heat has left the test tube.
options.rationale: Students hear 'energy has gone' and reach for exothermic, without asking which way it moved relative to the surroundings.

options.text: The reaction is destroying energy, so less is left in the tube.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think reactions consume energy rather than transfer it, so a fall in temperature looks like destruction.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an endothermic reaction?

options.text: The combustion of methane in a Bunsen flame
options.rationale: Students who focus on having to light the burner conclude that burning takes energy in overall.

options.text: The neutralisation of nitric acid by an alkali
options.rationale: 'Neutral' suggests nothing happening, so neutralisation is imagined as a cancelling out rather than an exothermic reaction.

options.text: The oxidation of iron inside a hand warmer
options.rationale: Chosen by students who associate rusting with slow, quiet change and assume slow reactions must absorb energy.

options.text: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
options.rationale: The specification lists thermal decompositions as endothermic: energy has to be taken in from the surroundings for them to proceed.

mcqs.stem: Citric acid solution is stirred into sodium hydrogencarbonate. The mixture fizzes and the temperature falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is exothermic; the fizzing shows energy is being given out.
options.rationale: Bubbling looks dramatic, and students associate visible activity with energy being released rather than with the rate.

options.text: The reaction has released cold into the solution, lowering its reading.
options.rationale: Heat and cold are treated as opposite substances in everyday speech, so cooling is explained as cold coming out.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic; the escaping gas carries the energy away.
options.rationale: A mechanical explanation that matches steam leaving a pan, and it avoids accepting that a reaction can absorb energy.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic; it has taken energy from the surroundings.
options.rationale: The temperature of the surroundings has decreased, which is the specification's criterion for an endothermic reaction.

mcqs.stem: A student mixes two solutions in a polystyrene cup. The thermometer reading rises from 19 °C to 27 °C. What can be concluded?

options.text: The reaction is endothermic; energy has moved into the solution.
options.rationale: Students who think a warming object must be absorbing energy reverse the two definitions in exactly this way.

options.text: The reaction is exothermic; the surroundings have become warmer.
options.rationale: The solution is the surroundings here, and its temperature has increased, so energy has been transferred to the surroundings.

options.text: Nothing about energy; a rise only shows the reaction was fast.
options.rationale: Rate and energy change are met in the same practical work, so a temperature rise gets read as a measure of speed.

options.text: The solution warmed because stirring transferred energy into it.
options.rationale: Chosen by students looking for a physical cause; stirring cannot account for an 8 °C rise in a small volume.

mcqs.stem: Four reactions were carried out in identical insulated cups. The solution temperature changed as follows: W, 20 °C to 31 °C; X, 20 °C to 14 °C; Y, 20 °C to 20 °C; Z, 20 °C to 26 °C. Which reaction is endothermic?

options.text: W, because it produced the largest temperature change
options.rationale: Students trained to pick the largest value in a table compare magnitudes and never check the direction.

options.text: Z, because the temperature rose by only 6 °C
options.rationale: Selected by students who treat a small change as evidence of energy trickling in slowly rather than out.

options.text: X, because the temperature of the solution fell by 6 °C
options.rationale: Only X shows a decrease in the temperature of the surroundings, which is what defines an endothermic reaction.

options.text: Y, because no energy at all was transferred in it
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'takes in energy' as 'gives nothing out', so a flat reading looks endothermic.

mcqs.stem: Hand warmer A reaches 58 °C and lasts 1 hour, then must be thrown away. Hand warmer B reaches 42 °C, lasts 7 hours and can be reset in boiling water. Which is the better choice for a full day of hill walking?

options.text: B, because it stays warm all day and can then be used again.
options.rationale: The stated use is a full day, so duration and reusability outweigh a peak temperature that only lasts an hour.

options.text: A, because the higher temperature means more energy is given out.
options.rationale: Peak temperature is the single number students are used to comparing, so the hottest option looks best by default.

options.text: B, because its reaction is endothermic and so lasts far longer.
options.rationale: Right choice, wrong chemistry: a warmer that heats your hands is exothermic, whatever is done to reset it afterwards.

options.text: A, because B must be boiled in water before each separate use.
options.rationale: A real practical drawback, but B does not need boiling during the walk, so it does not decide this comparison.

mcqs.stem: A sports injury pack holds a solid and a sachet of water. Squeezing it mixes them and the pack cools to 2 °C in under a minute. Which is the strongest reason for keeping this pack in a pitch-side first aid kit?

options.text: It releases cold into the injury, which an ice pack cannot do.
options.rationale: Treats cold as a substance that flows outwards, a description students use freely in everyday speech.

options.text: Its endothermic reaction transfers energy into the injured area.
options.rationale: Reverses the direction of transfer; an endothermic reaction takes energy from the surroundings, including the skin.

options.text: It needs no freezer, works at once and can be carried anywhere.
options.rationale: The endothermic reaction produces the cooling on demand, which is exactly what a portable kit away from a freezer requires.

options.text: It can be squeezed and re-used many times during a single match.
options.rationale: Attractive because reusability sounds like an advantage, but once the reactants have mixed the pack cannot be reset.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 4 a student adds sodium hydroxide solution to 30 cm3 of hydrochloric acid in 5 cm3 portions, recording the highest temperature after each addition. What is the independent variable?

options.text: The highest temperature reached each time
options.rationale: The measured quantity fills the results table, so it feels like the important and therefore the independent variable.

options.text: The volume of hydrochloric acid in the cup
options.rationale: Students who think a fair test means increasing everything together expect the acid volume to change as well.

options.text: The concentration of the sodium hydroxide
options.rationale: Picked by students who spot 'sodium hydroxide' in the method and choose the first property of it they can name.

options.text: The volume of sodium hydroxide added
options.rationale: This is the quantity the student deliberately changes from one reading to the next, which is what makes it independent.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 4 the reacting solutions are mixed in a polystyrene cup fitted with a lid. Why?

options.text: Polystyrene does not react with acids, unlike a glass beaker does.
options.rationale: Choosing apparatus for chemical resistance is a familiar habit, and glass is unreactive too, so the reasoning is never tested.

options.text: It makes the reaction give out more energy than it otherwise would.
options.rationale: The reading really is bigger with a lid on, and the simplest explanation of a bigger reading is a bigger reaction.

options.text: It reduces energy transfer between the mixture and the surroundings.
options.rationale: Polystyrene is a poor conductor and the lid stops energy escaping upwards, so the measured temperature change is closer to the true value.

options.text: It holds the mixture at a constant temperature while it is reacting.
options.rationale: Sounds like good practice, but a constant temperature would leave nothing for the student to measure.

mcqs.stem: What must be true for two reacting particles to react when they meet?

options.text: They must collide with each other; any collision will do it.
options.rationale: The collision picture is intuitive and the energy condition is an extra clause that is easy to drop.

options.text: Every particle must first be raised to the activation energy.
options.rationale: Students treat the activation energy as a threshold for the whole sample, as though it were a melting point.

options.text: They must gain energy equal to the overall energy change.
options.rationale: Confuses the barrier that must be climbed with the difference in energy between reactants and products.

options.text: They must collide with each other, and with sufficient energy.
options.rationale: The specification gives both conditions: reactions occur only when particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

mcqs.stem: What is the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: The minimum energy that particles must have in order to react
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of activation energy, stated as the minimum amount of energy particles must have to react.

options.text: The energy that is given out once the reaction has started
options.rationale: The word 'activation' suggests the reaction springing into life, which students associate with energy coming out.

options.text: The difference in energy between the reactants and products
options.rationale: Both quantities are vertical distances in kJ/mol on the same diagram, so they are easily swapped.

options.text: The energy needed to raise the mixture by one degree
options.rationale: Imports a definition from energy calculations in physics, which sounds technical and therefore plausible.

mcqs.stem: What can be read directly from a reaction profile?

options.text: The time taken by the reaction and the rate at each moment of it
options.rationale: Almost every other graph in science has time along the bottom, so the horizontal axis is read as time.

options.text: The relative energies of reactants and products and the activation energy
options.rationale: The specification says reaction profiles show the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change.

options.text: The temperature of the surroundings before and after the reaction
options.rationale: Temperature is the quantity used throughout 4.5.1.1, so students expect to see it on the vertical axis.

options.text: The mass of each reactant and the mass of each product formed
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect any chemistry diagram to carry quantitative information about amounts.

mcqs.stem: A student is drawing a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction. Which description is correct?

options.text: The products are drawn above the reactants, with a curve peaking above both.
options.rationale: 'Giving out energy' is heard as 'having more', and higher on the diagram is read as more of everything.

options.text: The products are drawn below the reactants, with a straight line sloping down.
options.rationale: Students see the diagram as a comparison of two levels and treat the joining line as decoration.

options.text: The products are drawn below the reactants, with a curve peaking above both.
options.rationale: The products have less energy than the reactants, and the curved line must rise to a peak so that the activation energy can be shown.

options.text: The products are drawn level with the reactants, with a curve dipping below.
options.rationale: Attractive to students who think 'exothermic' means the energy dips down during the reaction and then returns.

mcqs.stem: On a reaction profile the reactants are at 250 kJ/mol, the peak of the curve is at 400 kJ/mol and the products are at 310 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Endothermic; the activation energy is 400 kJ/mol.
options.rationale: Reads the height of the peak from the axis upwards, in the way heights are normally read off a graph.

options.text: Endothermic; the activation energy is 60 kJ/mol.
options.rationale: Gives the overall energy change instead, confusing the two vertical distances on the same diagram.

options.text: Exothermic; the activation energy is 150 kJ/mol.
options.rationale: Students who expect exothermic profiles to rise from left to right label this one exothermic despite the products being higher.

options.text: Endothermic; the activation energy is 150 kJ/mol.
options.rationale: The products are above the reactants, so energy was taken in, and the activation energy is the climb from 250 to 400 kJ/mol.

mcqs.stem: A mixture of methane and air can sit unchanged in a laboratory until a spark is applied, after which it burns. What does the spark supply?

options.text: The activation energy, the energy needed for the reaction to occur
options.rationale: The activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur, and until it is supplied no collisions are successful.

options.text: The energy that the burning reaction will give out afterwards
options.rationale: Treats the activation energy as the energy the reaction produces rather than the energy it requires first.

options.text: The energy difference between the methane and the products
options.rationale: Substitutes the overall energy change for the barrier, since both are energies attached to the same reaction.

options.text: The energy that only endothermic reactions normally require
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe an exothermic reaction has energy to spare and so needs none putting in.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about bonds during a chemical reaction is correct?

options.text: Energy is released when bonds break; energy must be supplied to form bonds.
options.rationale: Everyday talk about energy 'stored in bonds' being released when they break says exactly this.

options.text: Energy must be supplied both to break bonds and to form the new bonds.
options.rationale: Students generalise from the activation energy that every step of a reaction needs energy putting in.

options.text: Energy is released both when bonds break and when the new bonds form.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think any reaction that gets hot must be releasing energy at every stage.

options.text: Energy must be supplied to break bonds; energy is released when bonds form.
options.rationale: This is the specification's statement of what happens during a reaction: bond breaking requires energy, bond making releases it.

mcqs.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242, H-Cl 431. For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, what is the total energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants?

options.text: 862 kJ/mol
options.rationale: This is 2 x 431, the energy released forming the product bonds, taken from the wrong side of the equation.

options.text: 678 kJ/mol
options.rationale: One H-H bond and one Cl-Cl bond are broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol.

options.text: 431 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Uses a single bond energy from the table without working out which bonds are actually present or how many.

options.text: 184 kJ/mol
options.rationale: The overall energy change, given by a student who completes the whole calculation without reading what was asked.

mcqs.stem: Bond energies in kJ/mol: H-H 436, Br-Br 193, H-Br 366. What is the overall energy change for H2 + Br2 → 2HBr?

options.text: +103 kJ/mol
options.rationale: The right magnitude with the subtraction reversed, done to avoid a negative answer.

options.text: -103 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Bonds broken 436 + 193 = 629; bonds formed 2 x 366 = 732; overall change 629 - 732 = -103 kJ/mol, so the reaction is exothermic.

options.text: +263 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Counts only one H-Br bond (629 - 366), ignoring the 2 in front of HBr in the balanced equation.

options.text: -1361 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Adds every bond energy in the table instead of finding the difference between the two sums.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of an exothermic reaction?

options.text: The energy needed to break bonds is greater than that released making them.
options.rationale: This is the condition for an endothermic reaction, chosen when the two sums are subtracted the wrong way round.

options.text: The energy released making bonds is greater than that needed to break them.
options.rationale: This is the specification's statement: in an exothermic reaction the energy released from forming new bonds exceeds the energy needed to break existing bonds.

options.text: Energy is released when bonds break and taken in when new bonds form.
options.rationale: Reverses both processes, following the everyday idea that breaking a bond lets stored energy out.

options.text: The products simply contain more separate bonds than the reactants do.
options.rationale: Counting bonds is easier than adding energies and often gives the right answer, so the shortcut persists.

mcqs.stem: In a reaction, breaking the bonds in the reactants needs 2560 kJ/mol and forming the bonds in the products releases 2380 kJ/mol. What is the overall energy change, and what type of reaction is it?

options.text: Endothermic, with an overall energy change of +180 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Bonds broken minus bonds formed is 2560 - 2380 = +180 kJ/mol; more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making them.

options.text: Exothermic, with an overall energy change of -180 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Subtracts the sums the other way round, then reads the negative sign as exothermic.

options.text: Exothermic, with an overall energy change of +180 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Gets the arithmetic right but classifies it by the belief that bond breaking is what releases energy.

options.text: Endothermic, with an overall energy change of 4940 kJ/mol
options.rationale: Adds the two figures instead of finding the difference between them, while classifying the reaction correctly.
